plan.analysis: The flat start gives exactly 2/3. Key insight: f(x)=x^(-1/2) on [0,1] gives (f*f)(x)=pi exactly on [0,1], with a decaying tail on [1,2]; saddle-point estimate of the integrals gives integral(g^2)~11.2, mass=4, max=pi, i.e. R~0.89, far above 2/3. That is the main bet. Second bet: numerically polish that shape (coordinate ascent in log-heights, coarse-to-fine). Third bet: tame the costly tail by modulating the right end with (1-x)^beta (and a small offset c at the singular end) — a smooth 2-parameter family around the analytic point, scanned cheaply.

experiments.hypothesis: f(x)=x^(-1/2) has f*f exactly flat (=pi) on [0,1]; the only loss is the small tail on [1,2], so R should jump from 2/3 to ~0.89.
experiments.change: Ignore start. Build h of length N with h[i] = ((i+0.5)/N)^(-1/2) on [0,1]. To use the budget: loop over N in {2000, 8000, 32000} and over knot conventions k in {0.0, 0.5} with h[i]=((i+k)/N)^(-1/2) (skip k=0 on i=0 if it gives inf, then clip finite), compute R from L=[0,*convolve(h,h),0] exactly via the stated formula, print each R, and return the best h. Use fftconvolve (numpy rfft) if plain convolve is too slow for N=32000.
experiments.prediction: Best R ~ 0.885-0.895, confirming the plateau-plus-small-tail picture (no tail would give 1; a triangle gives 2/3).

experiments.hypothesis: The analytic shape is not optimal; the tail can be partly traded against a very slightly non-flat plateau, and local hill-climbing in log-h on a fine grid will find that trade, raising R above 0.89.
experiments.change: Ignore start. Initialize h[i]=((i+0.5)/N)^(-1/2). Then run a coarse-to-fine multiplicative coordinate ascent that uses nearly the whole budget: for N in [64,128,256,512,1024,2048,4096] resample current shape onto N steps, then do sweeps over all coordinates, proposing h[i]*exp(+delta) and h[i]*exp(-delta) (accept the better only if R increases), with delta starting at 0.2 and halving each sweep, ~8 sweeps per scale, and stop when time.process_time() > budget_seconds-1.5, returning the best h seen at the finest scale. Evaluate R with rfft-based convolution and the exact L=[0,conv,0] formula; print R after each scale.
experiments.prediction: R increases monotonically with scale and ends at ~0.90-0.92, with the optimum having a tiny elevation of h near i=0 and a slightly depressed h just before the right end.

experiments.hypothesis: All the loss comes from the tail on [1,2]; multiplying f by (1-x)^beta pushes the right endpoint to 0 and shrinks that tail, while the plateau only dips slightly for small beta, so some beta>0 should beat beta=0.
experiments.change: Ignore start. For N=2000 build h[i] = ((i+0.5)/N + c)^(-1/2) * (1-(i+0.5)/N)^beta, scan the grid c in {0,1e-4,1e-3,1e-2} x beta in {0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2,0.25,0.3}, print all R values and the top five; then spend the remaining time on a fine scan of beta in [best-0.05, best+0.05] with 25 equally spaced values at the best c (and N=8000 for the final best), returning the best h found. Compute R exactly from L=[0,*convolve(h,h),0].
experiments.prediction: Best R ~0.89-0.91 at small beta (~0.05-0.12), clearly above the beta=0 value ~0.888; large beta (>0.2) will fall below 2/3's neighbourhood of 0.888 because the plateau dip dominates.

plan.analysis: p0006 is very close to the continuous x^{-1/2} limit 4 ln 2 / π ≈ 0.882542, so gains are now small. The strongest line is refining the step-function approximation of the singularity at 0 and the tail. p0005's local search and p0007's tapering both failed, so I avoid repeating those. I bet on: (1) higher resolution with exact cell averages, (2) tuning the first few heights to better fit the singular profile, (3) a new multiplicative tilt that increases f near 1 (opposite of p0007's taper) to see if the tail can be boosted.

experiments.hypothesis: The continuous x^{-1/2} gives R ≈ 0.882542; p0006 at N=32000 is 0.882389. Increasing N and using exact cell averages instead of midpoint values should reduce discretization error and approach the limit.
experiments.change: Set N=200000. Compute heights as exact cell averages of x^{-1/2}: h[i] = 2*N*(sqrt((i+1)/N) - sqrt(i/N)) for i=0..N-1. Also compute midpoint h[i]=((i+0.5)/N)^-0.5, evaluate both with _R_from_h, and return the better array. Keep the same scoring function.
experiments.prediction: R will be between 0.88245 and 0.88255, improving on 0.882389.

experiments.hypothesis: The step-function approximation of x^{-1/2} near 0 is not optimal for finite N; tuning the first few heights can better trade the singular ramp against the plateau, potentially exceeding the continuous limit.
experiments.change: Start from p0006's best h (N=32000, k=0). Run 5 passes of coordinate ascent over the first 10 indices: for each idx in 0..9, try multiplying h[idx] by factors [0.9, 0.95, 0.98, 1.02, 1.05, 1.1], keep the change if exact R improves. Return the best h found.
experiments.prediction: R will increase by at least 0.00005, possibly reaching 0.88250 or higher.

experiments.hypothesis: p0007's taper (1-x)^β decreased f near 1 and hurt. The opposite perturbation, increasing f near 1 via (1 + c x), may raise the tail of f*f enough to increase L2^2 without raising Linf too much.
experiments.change: Generate h[i] = ((i+0.5)/N)^-0.5 * (1 + c * ((i+0.5)/N)) for N=32000. Sweep c over np.linspace(-0.5, 0.5, 101). Evaluate exact R for each, print the best few, and return the best h. If time remains, also try the window (1 + c*(1-x)).
experiments.prediction: If increasing near 1 helps, the best c will be positive and R > 0.8825; otherwise the best c will be near 0 and R ≈ 0.8824.

plan.analysis: x^{-1/2} is the unique power making f*f exactly flat on [0,1]; the residual loss is the tail on [1,2], so the continuous value 0.882542 is the target and any gain is small. p0012's first-10 coordinate ascent closed most of the finite-N gap (0.882520). Bet: (a) a true gradient over all heights squeezes the finite-N optimum better than coordinate ascent, (b) higher resolution with a tuned singularity and right end recovers the continuous limit, (c) smooth multiplicative corrections test whether x^{-1/2} is a genuine local max. The gradient and high-N lines have the best upside; the smooth family is the exploratory bet.

experiments.hypothesis: p0012 only tuned the first 10 heights; the right end (near x=1) controls the [1,2] tail, and finer factors / more indices can still gain.
experiments.change: Take start (N=32000). Run multiplicative coordinate ascent cycling over index sets A={0..29} and B={N-30..N-1}, factor grid {0.90,0.95,0.98,0.99,0.995,1.005,1.01,1.02,1.05,1.10}; keep the best h after each full pass, repeat passes until 0.9*budget_seconds. Return best h.
experiments.prediction: R rises modestly above 0.882520 (target >=0.88253), confirming tuning beyond the first 10 and at the right end helps.

experiments.hypothesis: The continuous x^{-1/2} gives 0.882542 but point-sampling at N=32000 loses ~1.5e-4; a much finer grid with a tuned singularity region and tuned right end should approach the continuous limit.
experiments.change: Ignore start's exact values; build fresh h of length N=200000 with h[i]=((i+0.5)/N)^(-0.5). Then run multiplicative coordinate ascent over the first 200 and last 200 indices with factor grid {0.9,0.95,0.98,0.99,1.01,1.02,1.05,1.1}, multiple passes until 0.9*budget_seconds. Return best h.
experiments.prediction: Reaches ~0.88254, at or above p0012's 0.882520, showing higher resolution plus tuned singularity/right end recovers the continuous-limit value.

experiments.hypothesis: Coordinate ascent is a weak local optimizer; the exact gradient of R w.r.t. all heights, with projection to h>=0, can reach a better finite-N local maximum.
experiments.change: Take start (N=32000). Implement projected gradient ascent using the analytic gradient: c=conv(h,h) via FFT, L=[0,c,0]; M=(1/3)sum(L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2); S=sum(h), L1=S^2, Linf=max(L), j*=argmax. Set d_k=(4L_k+L_{k-1}+L_{k+1})/3 (out-of-range L=0). gradM_i=2*correlate(d[1:2N], h)_i; gradL1_i=2S; gradLinf_i=2*h[j*-1-i] (0 if out of range). gradR=(gradM*L1*Linf - M*(gradL1*Linf+L1*gradLinf))/(L1*Linf)^2. Update h<-max(0, h + eta*gradR) with backtracking line search on eta (halve until R improves); keep best h; iterate with shrinking steps until 0.9*budget. Return best h.
experiments.prediction: Gradient ascent beats coordinate ascent: R>0.882520, ideally >=0.88254; if it stalls at 0.882520 it confirms p0012 sits at a local optimum.

plan.analysis: p0017 is only 1.1e-5 below the continuous x^{-1/2} value 0.882542, but its search tunes only the first/last 30 heights. The evidence suggests remaining loss is either finite-N discretization or a slightly non-x^{-1/2} shape. I will bet on three directions: exact full-gradient refinement of p0017; a corrected cell-average discretization at N=200000 on the p0019 fine-grid branch; and a low-dimensional global search over smooth multiplicative perturbations of x^{-1/2} to test whether the extremal shape is truly x^{-1/2}.

experiments.hypothesis: p0017 only tunes the first and last 30 heights; the interior may still have a small gradient. Exact full-length gradient ascent should find any remaining local improvement and use the whole budget.
experiments.change: Replace p0017's coordinate sweep with projected gradient ascent on all N heights. Compute L=convolve(h,h) via FFT with zero padding. Let A=sum(L_j^2+L_j L_{j+1}+L_{j+1}^2)/3, B=(sum h)^2, C=max L at index m. Set g_j=(L_{j-1}+4L_j+L_{j+1})/3. Compute dA/dh_i=2*sum_j g_j h_{j-i} by FFT correlation, dB/dh_i=2*sum(h), dC/dh_i=2*h_{m-i}. Then dR=(dA*B*C - A*(dB*C+B*dC))/(B*C)^2. Update h=max(0,h+step*dR) with backtracking line search, renormalize mean to 1, and continue until 95% of budget. Verify the gradient against finite differences on a small N first.
experiments.prediction: R rises above p0017 to at least 0.88254 (+1e-5), showing interior heights were left on the table; if it stalls exactly at 0.882531, p0017 is already a full gradient optimum.

experiments.hypothesis: p0019 tested a finer grid but still lost to point-sampling error. Exact cell averages of x^{-1/2} are the correct step-function projection and should recover the continuous value 0.882542.
experiments.change: Take p0019's N; if N<200000, resample to N=200000. Replace the heights by exact cell averages of x^{-1/2}: h_i = 2*N*(sqrt((i+1)/N)-sqrt(i/N)) for i=0..N-1. Then apply p0017's first/last 30 multiplicative coordinate tuning to this array and keep the best. Use the full budget, stopping only at 95%.
experiments.prediction: Score reaches about 0.88254 and beats p0017, confirming discretization was the loss. If it stays below p0017, cell-averaging alone is not the missing correction.

experiments.hypothesis: The true extremal may not be exactly x^{-1/2}; a smooth low-dimensional perturbation can escape the local basin while remaining close enough to keep the flat convolution plateau.
experiments.change: Parameterize h_i = x_i^{-1/2} * exp(sum_{k=1}^{K} c_k T_k(2x_i-1)), where x_i=(i+0.5)/N, T_k are Chebyshev polynomials, K=8, and c_k in [-0.2,0.2]. Use N=4000 for search. Maximize R over c with scipy.optimize.minimize(method='Powell') from 5 random starts plus c=0. Take the best c, resample to N=32000, and run p0017's first/last 30 coordinate tuning. Use the full budget.
experiments.prediction: Either a new best >0.88255 from a non-x^{-1/2} shape, or all starts return c≈0 and R≈0.88252, supporting x^{-1/2} as a strong local/global attractor.

plan.analysis: p0025 is at a local plateau: coordinate and log-gradient ascent give only +1e-5, with f*f nearly flat and max at 0.096 support. The remaining gains likely come from (i) finer discretization near the singular endpoint, (ii) fixing p0025's omitted active-Lmax gradient term, and (iii) testing whether the sub-maximal autoconvolution tail can be filled by a right-end block. These are one refinement, one optimizer correction, and one genuinely different shape bet.

experiments.hypothesis: At N=32000 the step approximation still limits R; doubling N with duplicated heights gives extra degrees of freedom to resolve the x^{-1/2} endpoint and the tuned right end more accurately.
experiments.change: In construct, take h0=start, build h=np.repeat(h0,2) (N=64000), so the initial step function and R are unchanged. Run p0025's _R_from_h, then its coordinate ascent on the first 80 and last 80 indices, then its log-space gradient ascent with the same backtracking schedule, keeping the best exact R. Use the full budget up to 28 s CPU.
experiments.prediction: Score improves slightly above 0.882531, showing discretization error was still active; if unchanged, N=32000 is already converged.

experiments.hypothesis: p0025's gradient ignores dLmax/dh, so ascent is not following the true constrained gradient; including the active maximum knot(s) should improve the local optimum.
experiments.change: Modify _gradient_update to compute Lmax and the set of active indices m with L[m] >= Lmax*(1-1e-12). Add dLmax/dh_k = average over active m of 2*h[m-1-k] for valid indices. Change the gradient to dR = dS2/(3*S1*Lmax) - R/S1 - (R/Lmax)*dLmax. Keep the same log-space normalization and exact-R backtracking, run until 28 s CPU, and return the best h.
experiments.prediction: A measurable gain over 0.882531, at least ~1e-6, confirming the omitted Lmax term was slowing convergence.

experiments.hypothesis: The autoconvolution tail on [1,2] is below the maximum; appending a narrow right-end block can raise L2 there without raising the [0,1] plateau, if its height is tuned to stay under Lmax.
experiments.change: Start from p0025 h (N=32000). For M in {160,320,640,1280} and A in {0.25,0.5,1,2,4} times the mean of h[-100:], form h_ext = concatenate(h, A*ones(M)). Compute exact R for each h_ext, pick the best extended array (or keep original if all worse), then run p0025's coordinate and log-gradient ascent on h_ext until 28 s CPU. Return the best array seen.
experiments.prediction: Either a new higher score if the tail has room, or no gain, which would show the right-end tail is already saturated near the optimum.

experiments.hypothesis: The exact-gradient code uses only the first argmax knot on the flat max plateau, which biases the Lmax derivative and can stall ascent. Averaging the subgradient over the whole near-max plateau should remove this bias.
experiments.change: In _eval_grad, replace m_idx=int(argmax(L)) with up to 100 evenly spaced indices j where L[j] >= C*(1-1e-6). experiments.prediction: If plateau bias was limiting, R rises slightly above 0.882531; otherwise the score stays identical.

experiments.hypothesis: x^{-1/2} may be only a local maximum. Random multiplicative perturbations and alternative power-law starts can reach different basins that local gradient ascent from the start misses.
experiments.change: Wrap the existing gradient ascent in an outer restart loop. After each convergence, if time remains, set h_new = best_h * exp(0.1*randn(n)), clip to >=0, normalize mean to 1, and rerun ascent for up to 200 iterations. Every third restart instead use h_i = ((i+0.5)/N)^-α with α uniform in [0.45,0.55] times exp(0.05*randn(n)). Keep the best R; use deadline 0.93*budget.
experiments.prediction: Either finds a better basin with R>0.882531, or all restarts return to the same value, confirming a strong local max.
